item.title: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
item.description:
Ukrainian president says Kyiv not ready to concede Donbas but would put idea to a referendum in exchange for security guarantees and funding. What we know on day 1,726

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member. But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded ​Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a ‌national referendum. Echoing comments ‌made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are ‌agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. “We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

The Ukrainian president has also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, something that could only happen if the country’s constitution was changed. “If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in Nato right now anyway.”

US President ⁠Donald Trump’s ⁠envoy and ​son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner said on ⁠Saturday ​the US ‌was ‌focused on ‌facilitating direct engagement between Russia and ‌European nations on ​the Ukraine war, ⁠after trilateral meetings ​involving Washington, ​Moscow ​and ​Kyiv ‌this ​week. However, Washington and Nato have not yet commented on the suggestion of a swap of the Donbas for Ukraine Nato membership. Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.

Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system, saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones, in place for five days, meant they could no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Putin.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an “unjust peace” and warned that it was a recipe for another war. “Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said on social media. “That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France’s position.”

Russian forces ⁠struck a cargo vessel in ⁠the ⁠Ukrainian ​port of Chornomorsk, RIA ⁠news agency cited the Russian ⁠defence ministry ​as ‌saying on ‌Saturday. The ministry ‌said the ship was being used to supply the Ukrainian ‌military. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region on Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. Separately, 22 people were injured in a Russian attack on the south-east Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

item.title: Grocery giant Aldi recalls tortelloni over potentially ‘life-threatening’ health risks: Avoid these products
item.description:
Aldi has issued a recall due to the potential presence of Clostridium botulinum. 

Two tortellini products from the Illinois-based grocery store chain’s Priano brand might contain the life-threatening bacteria, according to a recall notice from Aldi that was reposted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Clostridium botulinum, or C. botulinum, can cause botulism, a very dangerous form of food poisoning.

According to the notice, the potential contamination resulted because the products may have been stored, distributed, or sold at improper temperatures.  

Here’s what you need to know about the Aldi recall. 

What products are affected?

The Aldi recall is for two types of its tortellini:

Priano Protein Carbonara Tortelloni, 9 oz, plastic unit 

  • Lot number: T9101926
  • Best-by date: December 18, 2026

Priano Protein Herb & Cheese Tortelloni, 9 oz, plastic unit

  • Lot number: T9101926
  • Best-by date: December 18, 2026

Where and when was the product sold?

The announcement doesn’t say exactly when the tortellini products were sold, but we do know where. Aldi sold the recalled products in-store and online from stores in the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Georgia
  • North Carolina 
  • South Carolina

What should I do if I have this product? 

You should either throw out the recalled tortellini or return it to Aldi for a full refund. “Consumers are warned not to prepare or consume the affected products from the impacted states, even if they do not look or smell spoiled,” the announcement states.

You can contact Aldi with any questions at (844) 484-0332 from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET, Monday to Friday. 

What botulism signs should I look out for? 

Get medical attention immediately if you’ve eaten the recalled tortellini and experience any of the following symptoms of botulism: 

  • Abdominal distension
  • Constipation
  • Difficulty breathing
  • Dizziness
  • Double vision
  • General weakness
  • Muscle weakness
  • Trouble speaking or swallowing

The franchisee, Tasty Chick’n LLC, operated 75 KFC restaurants and another nine cobranded KFC/Taco Bell locations across 10 states at the time of its bankruptcy petition.

But it also disclosed a list of more than 70 restaurants whose operations it did not deem worthy of continuing.

Those restaurants—many of which appear to have closed before the bankruptcy petition—are located in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Virginia.

The Memphis area appears especially hard hit, with more than a dozen of the city’s KFC locations on the closure list.

Why did the franchisee file for bankruptcy?

Texas-based Tasty Chick’n and its affiliates say higher operating costs and declining revenue have eaten into their bottom line, with restaurant-level profitability declining since 2023. 

At the same time, the franchisee says costly demands for store upgrades from Yum Brands—parent company of KFC and Taco Bell—have led to $15.6 million in unpaid royalties owed to the restaurant giant.

The situation became so precarious that Yum Brands in September sent Tasty Chick’n a “notice of intent” to terminate the company’s franchise agreements, court filings say. The franchisee turned to the Chapter 11 process with the hope of selling its assets while it explores “other stand-alone restructuring alternatives.”

Fast Company reached out to Yum Brands and Tasty Chick’n for comment.

Which KFC restaurants have closed or are closing?

In court papers filed on Tuesday, Tasty Chick’n listed dozens of its restaurants that it says are closing soon, in the process of closing, or have already closed.

A cursory search of the addresses reveals that most of the stores are already marked as closed on Google, with some of the closures happening recently.

The company and its affiliates are now seeking court permission to get out of their lease obligations for the locations and abandon the properties.

TRG is not identified as a debtor in the Chapter 11 proceedings.

Why does this sound familiar? 

Tasty Chick’n is not the first large fast-food restaurant operator to seek Chapter 11 protection this year.

In September, the owner of more than 300 Wendy’s restaurants filed for bankruptcy after years of sales struggles and a contentious relationship with the chain’s parent company. Franchisees for Denny’s, Subway, Moe’s Southwest Grill, and others have made similar moves.

Collectively, these franchisees have closed hundreds of restaurants in 2026.

Is KFC in trouble?

It’s not having the best year. Yum Brands recently reported a third-quarter decline of 6% for KFC’s U.S. sales. The picture is rosier elsewhere in the world, particularly in markets like the Middle East and Asia, where KFC’s Q3 sales were up by double digits.

The brand has faced increased competition in the market, particularly among younger consumers who have gravitated toward trendier chains such as Dave’s Hot Chicken and Raising Cane’s.

As of this writing, shares of Yum Brands Inc (NYSE: YUM) were up roughly 6.31% year to date, slightly underperforming the S&P 500, which was up 7.25% over the same period.

item.title: Chase confirms cyberattack that may have exposed customer data. Here’s what we know
item.description:
Chase Bank isn’t doing much to reassure customers.

The bank said Thursday that third-party vendors were recently targeted in a cyberattack that resulted in a breach of some customer information. But there is “no connection” between this cyber attack and the outage earlier this week that saw customers unable to log in to their accounts, the bank posted on X.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” Chase said in the post, without specifying when the breach occurred.

JPMorgan Chase, parent company of the bank, was one of several financial institutions to experience outages on Monday that saw many customers unable to log in to their accounts for several hours. A string of high-profile outages in the past week has upended work and air travel, while keeping Americans locked out of various websites. Even a highly classified network for internal communications at the National Security Agency also experienced an outage.

Another day, another data breach shouldn’t surprise most Americans at this point. But paranoia has been proliferating online about a more coordinated takedown of our tech infrastructure—and even though Chase said the cyberattack and outage are unrelated, some people aren’t buying what the largest U.S. bank is saying.

The New York-based company previously blamed the disruptions on Monday on a “software bug” that was resolved and said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or a systemic issue. 

So to announce a cyberattack a few days later has only raised more questions. A spokesperson for JPMorganChase didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company.

Cybernews reported Thursday that the ransomware gang n0n dumped on the dark web the stolen data of some 16,000 JPMorganChase customers and employees on Thursday after a 48-hour ransom had passed. The hackers said it had allegedly stolen information related to Chase’s premium Reserve credit card program that’s marketed to affluent Americans, as the outlet reported.

The most popular comment on a subreddit discussing that news report came from a Redditor who posted: “We are being lied to by the government.” That sort of refrain has become increasingly common as people have become more paranoid that something more nefarious is happening. 

RUBIO TRIES TO REASSURE

As conspiracy theories have flourished online in the wake of these outages, that’s led some Americans to panic-buying items at Costco, as Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, a petition on Change.org to “demand full transparency” about these recent tech disruptions has yet to garner much support.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has seemingly taken on the task in the Trump administration of trying to calm the nerves of Americans. Speaking on Tuesday during a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump, Rubio said the government has “no evidence” of a link between the outages or that they’re the result of cyberattacks, as Politico reported. 

“We fully acknowledge that this is unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. “We have no evidence, no indications of any kind that these incidents are related to each other or that any of them have anything to do with a malign actor, with a cyber criminal.”

Iran war stretching fleet’s capacity, navy chief admits, as CBO finds estimated cost of new ships ‘unrealistically low’

The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.

The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian cargo ship hit by drone in Baltic Sea as Finland PM says conflict ‘spilling over’
item.description:
Vessel erupts in flames after strike in Gulf of Finland; Nato vows to defend ‘every inch’ of Polish territory. What we know on day 1,733

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.

Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”

The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.

“I can guarantee ⁠that Nato will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said in Warsaw on Saturday, after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in its territory on Friday. Poland accused the Kremlin of “intentional provocation” after the incident, as it occurred near where thousands of European troops allied with Ukraine were holding training exercises.

A meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles. “In the near future, we ​will receive ​strong support from our NATO ​allies to bolster the protection of our eastern ​border,” Polish defence minister ‌Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote ​on ​X on Saturday.

In Kyiv, residents say they are unbothered by Russian attacks on the city’s bridges, as Moscow tries to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, Dan Sabbagh reports. Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population. Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.
